title: "Here, read my book"
hook: the one given his record in his right hand says to everyone: here, read my book (69:19)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the inevitable, al-Haqqah, and your line, what is real. Did a maybe get sorted from the real things? Today, the same surah shows us someone on that day, holding a book. Day six hundred forty-four, the end of a week.

Remember getting a report card you were proud of? You didn't fold it up and hide it in your backpack. You held it out at the kitchen table. Look. Read this. Now remember the other kind, the one you hoped nobody would ask about. Same paper, opposite instinct. Surah al-Haqqah takes that feeling, the urge to show or to hide, and sets it on the Day of Judgment. One person is handed a book and turns to everyone around them, almost laughing with relief: here, read it.

Verse nineteen, in Pickthall's translation: "Then, as for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: Take, read my book!" The Arabic begins with haa'umu, a call that means here, take it, come and look. The record, kitab, is the book of a person's deeds. Elsewhere the Qur'an speaks of noble scribes, angels who write down what people do. In the Qur'an's picture, the right hand is the sign of a good outcome. And the person's next words, in verse twenty, are a confession of how they lived: I was sure I would meet my reckoning. They didn't get there by never thinking about the day. They got there by thinking about it all along. The verses go on to a high garden with fruit hanging low, and the words: eat and drink, in return for what you sent ahead in days gone by. Then the surah turns. The one given the book in his left hand says the opposite: oh, I wish I'd never been given my book, never known my account. My wealth didn't help me. My power is gone from me. Same book, opposite instinct. One holds it out. One wishes it didn't exist. Muslims believe this scene is real, and it's meant to shape ordinary days now. The question it plants is simple. If today were written down in a book you'd be handed later, which parts would you hold out to the room?
screen: `I WAS SURE I'D MEET MY RECKONING.`
`THE LEFT HAND: I WISH I'D NEVER.`

segments.voice: The practice: do something you'd be glad to be seen doing. Sit, and walk back through yesterday like pages in a book. Don't judge every line. Just notice which pages you'd hold out, a kindness, a job done well, a hard thing done honestly, and which you'd turn face down. Then look ahead to today, and choose one thing you'd be glad to have written: a call, a fair word, a promise kept. The bell holds the time.
Here. The first word of the joyful one in 69:19, given the record in the right hand: here, read my book. Today's word.

Your line: here, read my book. This week: look again, held by the merciful, by the pen, great character, the poor's share first, what is real. Today, do one thing you'd hold out to the room. Day six hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims believe each person's deeds are recorded and that on the Day of Judgment the record is given in the right hand or the left; many recall this when examining their day, and pray to be given their book in the right hand.

original.note: Arabic, 69:19: here, take, read my book! haa'umu is a call to come and look.

trapdoor: what you thought: a person happy with their grade.
what it means: on the Day of Judgment, the one given the record in the right hand holds it out with nothing to hide.
what a scholar hears: haa'umu is an interjection, 'here, take'; the verse ends kitabiyah with a pause letter that the left-hand reply echoes.
